A1.justification: Both PDFs describe 3D Vision-Language Gaussian Splatting. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, figures, and rotated tables, are readable and support reliable matching of retained and added material.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation, localization, ablation, and efficiency results on LERF, 3D-OVS, and Mip-NeRF 360.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds component-combination experiments, augmentation and geometry-sharing comparisons, additional scene evaluations, image-quality measurements, and per-category analyses.

M1.justification: The proposed self-attention fusion, separate semantic indicator, camera-view blending, and training objectives remain unchanged. Appendix A.1 clarifies the existing attention implementation; the additional parameter-sharing models are experimental variants, not revisions to the adopted method.

E1.justification: v2 adds the table and snacks scenes to 3D-OVS evaluation (Table 18) and explicitly evaluates color-image synthesis on retained LERF scenes. The three datasets, application domain, and principal segmentation/localization tasks remain the same.

E2.justification: The named benchmark comparators remain unchanged. v2 Table 13 adds an evaluated alternative augmentation strategy using pretrained 3DGS renderings and SAM/CLIP features. Newly cited LEGS and HUGS are not added as evaluated benchmark baselines.

E3.justification: The added experiments substantially extend evaluation design through component-combination controls, four geometry-sharing configurations, offline augmentation with 120 interpolated views, and PSNR/SSIM and storage measurements. The existing experiments retain their stated feature extractors, 15,000 training iterations, optimizer, hardware, and learning rates; these additions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained individual-component ablations, v2 tests combinations of all three contributions (Tables 9–10), alternative augmentation (Table 13), and how much geometry should be shared (Table 17). Figures 18–19 examine color-driven segmentation errors, Tables 24–28 quantify category-specific indicator benefits, and the efficiency analysis expands to include image-quality trade-offs.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or formal significance tests. The additional results continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial ablation, efficiency, image-quality, and per-category results, including 98.5 and 94.7 mIoU on table and snacks, respectively (Table 18). Headline benchmark averages remain unchanged. However, LERF tables swap the teatime and figurines headings without moving their numbers: Table 1 assigns 73.5/58.1 to figurines/teatime in v1 and teatime/figurines in v2. This changes scene attribution, not demonstrated performance.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and Equations 1–12 are retained without substantive changes. The added geometry-sharing and augmentation arguments are conceptual explanations supported by experiments, not new formal assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about cross-modal rasterization, semantic indicators, view-blending regularization, and superior open-vocabulary segmentation. The appendix supplies additional support without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: Appendices A.3.4–A.3.5 add substantive explanations of feature-generation costs, online versus offline augmentation, and why sparse semantic supervision requires shared geometry. A.4.4 interprets view blending through specific color-confusion cases, while A.5.2 addresses whether semantic learning compromises RGB fidelity. These substantially extend the rationale and trade-off discussion.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the cross-attention query/key/value assignments, discloses training-image counts and the offline augmentation procedure, and reports additional resource measurements. Its new reproducibility statement promises source-code release upon acceptance; the PDFs do not establish an actual release. Existing implementation settings and learning rates are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds LEGS (Yu et al., 2024a) and HUGS (Zhou et al., 2024a), including a brief description of HUGS in related work. The broader positioning against existing language-embedded scene representations remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative receives limited wording corrections and affiliation/header updates. v2 adds ethical and reproducibility statements and organizes the expanded appendix into numbered subsections, while retaining the main section sequence and most existing prose.

P2.justification: v2 merges v1 Tables 4, 5, and 7 into Table 4, relocates retained displays, and substantially expands the appendix tables. Figure 9 enlarges existing framework panels rather than introducing a new component; Figures 18–19 add case-study displays. New per-category tables use rotated layouts and color-coded improvements.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct measurements of RGB fidelity and tests of how much geometry should remain shared. v2 addresses these central questions through Tables 17 and 23, while component-combination and per-category analyses strengthen attribution and the translucent/reflective-object argument. These additions substantially improve evidential support despite unchanged headline averages. Reporting weaknesses remain: the scene-label swap is unexplained, and Table 13's 53.0 no-augmentation baseline is not reconciled with the 55.8 no-view-blending result in Table 5.
